summary:
Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, which carries a maximum of five years' imprisonment and has been applied to women as well as men. The provision is enforced: in September 2018 four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar on charges of "acts against the order of nature" after videos circulated, part of a wave of politically motivated detentions ahead of the 2019 elections.

A campaign to raise the penalty to 15 years has been running since 2020, with anti-LGBT forces pushing for the increase as of July 2024. The maximum sentence remains five years; the proposal has not been reported as enacted.

Violence against LGBT people is documented at state and non-state level. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report on Senegal listed violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the country's major human rights problems, alongside pre-electoral violence and torture. Reporting in 2024 describes abuses against LGBT people as commonplace.

The most severe documented incident is the November 2023 exhumation and burning of the body of Cheikh Fall, a 31-year-old man identified locally as gay, in the street outside the cemetery where he had been buried. Images from the scene show a crowd of several hundred gathered around the fire; four men were arrested in connection with the incident.

Public speech about homosexuality is also policed. Two men, a political activist and a preacher, were jailed and each fined 100,000 CFA francs after posting a video attacking politician Ousmane Sonko for giving a platform to a visiting French politician who expressed support for same-sex marriage.

For a trans visitor, visible trans presentation carries a realistic risk of arrest under Article 319 and of mob violence. There is no visible community infrastructure; Dakar's scene is deeply underground.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Senegal surges around political moments. The 2018 detentions in Dakar preceded the 2019 elections, and the 2024 jailings followed a politician's hospitality toward a foreign visitor who voiced support for same-sex marriage. Elections and opposition rivalry are reliable triggers for arrest waves, so timing a visit to a campaign period raises exposure.

The 2012 US State Department report places LGBT violence within a broader pattern that included pre-electoral violence and torture, indicating that the security forces documented for other abuses are the same apparatus that enforces Article 319.

The gap between the five-year statutory maximum and the 15-year figure demanded by campaigners since 2020 shows a legislature under pressure to escalate rather than relax penalties. Comparable West African states maintain similar colonial-era provisions, but Senegal's active enforcement and the exhumation case place it at the harder end of the regional range.

Non-state violence is not incidental to the legal regime. The November 2023 burning of Cheikh Fall's exhumed body drew a crowd of hundreds, and only four arrests followed an act witnessed at that scale.
localsOnly:
Residents face up to five years' imprisonment under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, and the charge has been brought against women as well as men. Detentions in Dakar in September 2018 show that the provision is used against people identified through circulated video, not only through police investigation.

Residents also face punishment for speech. The jailing and 100,000 CFA franc fines imposed on a political activist and a preacher for a video about Ousmane Sonko's reception of a French politician establish that commentary defending or appearing to defend homosexuality is itself prosecutable.

There is no visible community infrastructure in Dakar; organising, social venues and support networks operate underground. Reporting describes abuses against LGBT people as commonplace, and the November 2023 exhumation and burning of Cheikh Fall's body shows the scale of collective violence that can follow an outing, with a crowd of several hundred present and four arrests made.

The US State Department's 2012 human rights report on Senegal recorded violence and discrimination against LGBT persons as a major national human-rights problem, alongside pre-electoral violence and torture.
outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition and change of sex markers on documents are not addressed anywhere in the assembled sources; whether any route exists for a visitor or resident is unresolved here.

Entry and visa rules, border screening of passports, and any gender-marker mismatch procedure at Dakar airport are not sourced. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether travellers are screened on this basis.

Hate-crime provisions, anti-discrimination law, and whether the 2012 report's findings prompted any protection machinery are not covered. The inventory also does not address bathroom or facilities rules, healthcare access, or partner and marriage recognition beyond the criminal penalty.

Whether the campaign to raise the sentence to 15 years has produced legislation is unresolved: the July 2024 report describes a push, not an enactment, and no later source confirms the outcome. The precise date of the BBC report on the two jailings and Ousmane Sonko's official position at the time of that judgment are likewise not fixed in the inventory.
